title: Perceiving Compliance in Virtual Reality: Effects of Interaction Direction and Sensory Discrepancy on Visuo-Haptic Weighting
venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
imageAlt: Haptic and visual stiffness rendering with baseline, top-down, front-back, and side-to-side VR interaction configurations
summary: Investigating how interaction direction and differences between visual and haptic feedback affect the perception of compliance in virtual reality.
question: How do interaction direction and sensory discrepancy shape visuo-haptic weighting?
approach: The supplied overview contrasts haptic and visual stiffness rendering and illustrates baseline, top-down, front-back, and side-to-side interaction configurations. These provide the context for studying how visual and haptic cues contribute to perceived compliance.

highlights.title: Visual and haptic stiffness
highlights.text: The schematic distinguishes physical haptic stiffness from visually rendered stiffness, including cases where visual stiffness is higher or lower.

highlights.title: Interaction direction
highlights.text: The illustrated VR configurations include top-down, front-back, and side-to-side interactions alongside a baseline shape.

highlights.title: Sensory weighting
highlights.text: The research examines how direction and discrepancy between sensory cues relate to visuo-haptic weighting in compliance perception.

title: CineHaptic: Context-Aware Real-Time Audiovisual-to-Haptic Rendering System for In-Vehicle 4D Cinematic Experiences
venue: ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology
booktitle: Proceedings of the ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology
imageAlt: CineHaptic pipeline from audiovisual event localization, salience classification, and audio processing to seat-based haptic patterns for an in-car 4D experience
summary: A context-aware system that translates audiovisual content into real-time haptic feedback for in-vehicle 4D cinematic experiences.
question: How can audiovisual events become context-aware haptic feedback for an in-vehicle cinematic experience?
approach: The supplied system overview combines event sound localization, event salience classification, and audio signal processing. Event location, salience, and dynamics inform spatiotemporal haptic patterns delivered through a vehicle seat alongside video and audio.

highlights.title: Context-aware event information
highlights.text: Video and audio contribute information about event location, salience, and dynamics.

highlights.title: Spatiotemporal haptic rendering
highlights.text: The pipeline maps event information to haptic patterns distributed across the seat.

highlights.title: In-vehicle 4D experience
highlights.text: The illustrated application brings video, audio, and seat-based haptic feedback together in a cinematic experience inside a vehicle.

title: Representing Egocentric Directions with Torso-Applied Vibrotactile Stimuli
imageAlt: Torso-based vibrotactile display for azimuth and elevation cues
summary: How can vibrations on the torso communicate directions in 3D space? Four perceptual experiments connect tactile locations to perceived azimuth and elevation.
question: A vibration has a location on the skin, but what direction does it suggest in the space around us?
approach: The study examines both stimulus identification and direction association, using physical vibrations and virtual locations created by the funneling illusion. Azimuth and elevation are evaluated within a shared experimental framework.

findings.title: More directions, fewer actuators
findings.text: Illusory stimuli can convey directional information while reducing the number of physical tactors.

findings.title: Perception has spatial biases
findings.text: Azimuth shows a lateral bias; elevation shows a downward bias on the back, particularly the upper back.

findings.title: A basis for directional rendering
findings.text: Regression models relate stimulus positions to perceived angles. Overall, azimuth cues communicate direction more effectively than elevation cues.

title: Human Identification Performance of Vibrotactile Stimuli Applied on the Torso Along Azimuth or Elevation
booktitle: Haptics: Understanding Touch; Technology and Systems; Applications and Interaction
imageAlt: Experimental torso layouts for identifying azimuth and elevation stimuli
summary: Measuring how accurately people identify horizontal and vertical tactile locations, and what happens when illusory stimuli double the available positions.
question: Does adding virtual tactile locations increase the information a torso display can communicate?
approach: Two absolute-identification experiments compare azimuth and elevation. Physical actuators provide real stimuli, and the funneling illusion adds intermediate locations.

findings.title: Reliable physical locations
findings.text: Identification accuracy exceeds 95.6% when physical stimuli represent six to eight directions.

findings.title: A resolution–accuracy trade-off
findings.text: Doubling the spatial resolution with illusory stimuli reduces accuracy to 74.1–77.8%.

findings.title: More locations do not guarantee more information
findings.text: Estimated information transfer remains similar across conditions, informing the design of torso-based navigation cues.

title: Telemetry-Based Haptic Rendering for Racing Game Experience Improvement
imageAlt: Telemetry-based haptic rendering pipeline and racing simulator
summary: Turning racing-game telemetry into tactile engine, collision, and road effects, with independent control over each part of the driving experience.
question: Can the state of a racing game provide more useful haptic effects than its mixed audio signal?
approach: A separate rendering process reads the game's exported telemetry. Engine, collision, and road effects are generated individually, combined with adjustable weights, and delivered through a haptic driving simulator.

findings.title: Effects tied to game events
findings.text: Separate telemetry signals allow engine, collision, and road sensations to be designed and adjusted individually.

findings.title: A working driving platform
findings.text: The system connects the rendering pipeline to bass shakers installed on the simulator and seat.

findings.title: User-experience evaluation
findings.text: Comparison with sound-based rendering examines the benefits and tuning trade-offs of telemetry-driven effects.

title: Information Transfer of Full-Body Vibrotactile Stimuli: An Initial Study with One to Three Sequential Vibrations
imageAlt: Full-body vibrotactile stimulation and sequential vibration patterns
summary: Quantifying how much information people can distinguish when one, two, or three vibrations are delivered in sequence across the body.
question: How does the length of a vibration sequence change the amount of information a person can recognize?
approach: Absolute-identification experiments compare sequences of one to three vibrations. Information-transfer estimates characterize a large stimulus set while accounting for the practical limits of experimental sampling.

findings.title: Sequence length as a design variable
findings.text: The study measures how distinguishable information changes with the number of sequential vibrations.

findings.title: Estimating a large stimulus space
findings.text: Combined estimation methods make it possible to study many patterns with a limited number of observations.

findings.title: Guidance for full-body messages
findings.text: Information capacity and commonly confused patterns help designers choose effective sequences. Frequency and intensity variation remain outside this study's scope.

title: Human Recognition Performance of Simple Spatial Vibrotactile Patterns on the Torso
imageAlt: Haptic vest and spatial vibration patterns on the front, back, and horizontal torso
summary: Investigating which simultaneous vibration patterns people can recognize on the torso, toward a practical vocabulary for haptic vests.
question: Which simple spatial patterns remain distinguishable when several torso actuators vibrate together?
approach: Sixteen on/off patterns are tested in front, back, and horizontal torso configurations. The study compares recognition across layouts and numbers of active motors.

findings.title: High overall recognition
findings.text: Recognition accuracy exceeds 91%, with performance varying by the number of active vibrations.

findings.title: A measurable tactile vocabulary
findings.text: Estimated information transfer is 3.48–3.66 bits, equivalent to roughly 11–12 perfectly distinguishable patterns.

findings.title: Patterns grounded in perception
findings.text: The results inform sets of distinguishable patterns for torso-based communication through haptic vests.
